parts.title: From recorder to real code: actions on a form

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 1 - Fundamentals - From recorder to real code: actions on a form

In Week 1, every action you wrote was `fill()` or `click()` on a login form with two fields. In this
lesson, you fill a whole registration form by hand: text fields, a radio button, checkboxes, and two
dropdowns. Then you write the same actions as a test in your own project, and end it with an
assertion.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Filling every kind of control on a registration form, and checking the result with an assertion. |
| **Goals** | Fill a text field, type into it one key at a time, check a radio button and a checkbox, pick an option in a dropdown, and find a control that has no label. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Week 1 - Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2) for locators, and [Week 1 - Day 5 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d5/p2) for assertions. |
| **Tools** | `fill()`, `pressSequentially()`, `check()`, `selectOption()`, `page.locator()`, and `toHaveValue`. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the examples, then your own project for the spec file. |
| **Key takeaway** | Each kind of control has one method that acts on it, and a test on a form ends with an assertion on the form. |

## The registration form

This lesson uses a practice page at
[demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html](https://demo.automationtesting.in/Register.html). It is
a registration form with no account behind it. Nothing you type is saved, so you can fill it as
often as you like. Selecting **Submit** on this page shows no confirmation message. The address
stays the same, and the fields keep their values. For that reason, the checks in this lesson look at
the fields themselves.

The form has three kinds of control that the login form did not have:

- A **radio button** is a small circle in a group, such as Male and FeMale under Gender. Selecting
  one clears the others, so a group holds one choice at a time.
- A **checkbox** is a small square, such as Cricket, Movies, and Hockey under Hobbies. Each one is
  on or off by itself, so you can check several.
- A **dropdown** is a list that opens when you select it, such as Skills and Select Country. You
  pick one of its options.

**Note:** The page spells the second gender option **FeMale**, with a capital M. The examples below
use the spelling that the page uses.

## Finding controls that have no label or placeholder

[Week 1 - Day 4 - Fundamentals](/learn/w1/d4/p2) introduced `getByPlaceholder`, `getByRole`, and
`getByLabel`. On this form, First Name and Last Name have placeholder text, and the two gender
radio buttons have labels. The other controls have no label, no placeholder, and no visible name,
so you need one more way to find an element.

An **attribute** is a name and a value written inside a tag, such as `type='email'` inside an
`<input>` tag. An **id** is an attribute that gives one element a name that no other element on the
page shares, such as `id="checkbox1"`.

`page.locator()` finds an element by a **CSS selector**, a short piece of text that describes an
element by its tag, its id, or one of its attributes:

| Selector | What it finds | Example on this form |
|---|---|---|
| `tag` | Every element with that tag | `page.locator('textarea')`, the Address field |
| `#id` | The element with that id | `page.locator('#checkbox1')`, the Cricket checkbox |
| `tag[attribute='value']` | Every element with that tag and that attribute value | `page.locator("input[type='email']")`, the Email field |

This form has one `<textarea>`, one `<input>` whose `type` is `email`, and one whose `type` is
`tel`, so each of those selectors finds exactly one element. Prefer a placeholder, a role, or a
label whenever a control has one. They describe what a user sees, and they keep working when the
page's markup changes. A selector describes the markup itself.

variation.prompt: Fill the form for yourself. Put your own first name and last name in the two name fields. Check Male and the Movies checkbox, whose id is checkbox2. Pick a skill other than Java and a country other than India, and show a screenshot.

blocks.text:
## Best practices

- Use `fill()` for text, and `pressSequentially()` only when a field reacts to each keystroke.
- Find a control by its placeholder, role, or label when it has one, and by a selector only when it
  has none.
- Read the exact text on the page before you write it into a locator, because `FeMale` is not
  `Female`.
- End every spec file with at least one assertion on the form, so that a step that went wrong makes
  the test fail.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | What you see | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Wrote `getByLabel('Male')` for the first radio button | An error that says the locator resolved to 2 elements, because Male also matches FeMale | Write `getByLabel('Male', { exact: true })`. |
| Used `#countries` for the country dropdown | `selectOption` waits, and then fails with a timeout | Use `#country`, the dropdown that holds the countries. |
| Selected two skills, expecting both to stay | Only the last pick is shown | Pick one skill. This dropdown holds one option at a time. |
| Wrote `.type()` from an older tutorial | VS Code draws a line through `type` | Write `pressSequentially()`, or `fill()` when the field does not react to each key. |
A search box shows suggestions after each letter that a user types. Which method fills it?

options: `fill()`, because it replaces the value in one step and is the usual choice
`pressSequentially()`, because the field reacts to each key
`selectOption()`, because the suggestions are a list of options to pick from
checkpoint.explanation: The suggestions appear only when the field sees a keystroke. `fill()` sets the value in one step, so the field sees no keystroke and shows nothing. `pressSequentially()` sends one key at a time, as a person typing would.

blocks.text: You call `selectOption('Java')` and then `selectOption('Python')` on the Skills dropdown. What is selected at the end?

options: Java and Python, because a dropdown keeps every option that was picked
Python only, because this dropdown holds one pick at a time
Java only, because the first pick is kept and every later pick is ignored
checkpoint.explanation: The Skills dropdown holds one option at a time, so the second pick replaces the first. A dropdown that keeps several picks is a different kind of control, and this form has none.

blocks.text: Why does `register.spec.ts` end with two `toHaveValue` assertions?

options: Because a test without an assertion passes even when a step went wrong
Because Playwright runs a spec file only when its last line is an `expect` call
Because `fill()` reports an error only when an assertion follows it in the same test
checkpoint.explanation: Each action proves only that its own step could be performed. Without a check on the form, a test passes whether or not the fields hold the right values. `fill()` reports an error on its own when it cannot find the field, so the assertion is not what makes it report errors.

blocks.text:
- `fill()` replaces the value of a text field in one step. `pressSequentially()` sends one key at a time, for a field that reacts to each keystroke.
- `check()` makes a radio button or a checkbox checked, and `selectOption()` picks one option in a dropdown.
- `page.locator()` finds a control by a **CSS selector** when it has no placeholder, role, or label: `#id` for an id, and `tag[attribute='value']` for an attribute.
- A test on a form ends with an assertion on the form, such as `toHaveValue` on a field that was filled.

## What's next

[Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3) moves these ten lines into one function, so that every test that
needs a filled form can call it.

parts.title: The same actions, the way a real project writes them

blocks.text:
# Week 2 - Day 1 - Implementation - The same actions, in one function

The test in [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2) fills the registration form in ten lines. In this
lesson, you move those ten lines into one function in a file of its own, and call it from two tests.
You do every step in VS Code and in its integrated terminal, in your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Moving the ten lines that fill the form into one function that every test can call. |
| **Goals** | Write a helper function in a file of its own, export it, import it into a spec file, and explain why the helper acts and the test asserts. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2), where you wrote the ten lines as a test. |
| **Tools** | `export`, `import type`, and a function with a `Page` parameter. |
| **Environment** | VS Code and its integrated terminal, in your project folder, then the editor on the right. |
| **Scope** | This lesson uses a plain function. The class-based Page Object Model is covered in a later lesson. |
| **Key takeaway** | Steps that several tests repeat belong in one function, and the assertions stay in the tests. |

## The problem with the Fundamentals version

Every test that needs a filled form has to repeat the same ten lines. Two tests hold the lines
twice, and a project with thirty such tests holds them thirty times. If the form gains a field, or
a placeholder changes, every copy needs the same edit. When the lines are written once, in one
function, you edit them once.

[Week 1 - Day 5 - Implementation](/learn/w1/d5/p3) solved the same problem for the sign-in steps
with a class. A form that one function can fill needs less than a class, so this lesson uses a plain
function.

## Why it is shaped this way

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| The helper acts, and the test asserts | Each test decides what the correct result is. A helper that checked for Ada's email could not serve the test for Grace. |
| The email is a parameter, and the other values are fixed | The email is the only value that the two tests need to differ. A parameter for every field would make each call as long as the ten lines it replaces. |
| The helper opens the page itself | A test that calls it needs one line to reach a filled form, with no `goto` to remember. |
| The file is named `registration-helpers.ts` | Playwright runs every file whose name ends in `.spec.ts`. This file has no tests, so it must not match that pattern. |

variation.prompt: Write the same kind of function in the editor. Complete fillNames so that it fills the First Name and Last Name fields with the two values it is given. Call it twice with two different names, and show a screenshot after the second call. The screenshot shows the second name, because fill() replaces the value that the first call entered.

blocks.text:
## What a reviewer looks for

- The steps that fill the form are written once, in `registration-helpers.ts`.
- The function is named for what it does, `fillRegistrationForm`, not for the methods inside it.
- The helper performs steps, and every assertion is in a test.
Why is the helper file named `registration-helpers.ts` and not `registration-helpers.spec.ts`?

options: Playwright runs every `.spec.ts` file, and this one contains no tests
TypeScript does not allow `export` in a file whose name ends in `.spec.ts`
The name of a helper file must end in `-helpers.ts` for an `import` line to find it
checkpoint.explanation: Playwright treats every file whose name ends in `.spec.ts` as a spec file and runs it. The helper contains no tests, so it must not match that pattern. `export` works in any file, and an `import` line finds a file by the path you write, whatever its name.

blocks.text: The helper takes the email as a parameter, but fills a fixed first name. Why?

options: The email is the one value that the two tests need to differ
A function can take only one parameter besides `page`, so one value had to be chosen
The website checks the first name, so it must be the same in every test
checkpoint.explanation: The two tests register two people, and only their emails differ. A parameter for every field would make each call as long as the ten lines it replaces. A function can take as many parameters as it needs.

blocks.text: Where do the assertions belong when a test calls `fillRegistrationForm`?

options: In the test, so that each test decides what the correct result is
In the helper, so that every test that calls it is checked in the same way
In both places, so that a mistake in either file is caught by the other one
checkpoint.explanation: The helper performs steps, and each test checks the result it expects. A helper that checked for Ada's email could not serve the test for Grace. Checking in both places would tie the helper to one expected result.

blocks.text:
- Steps that several tests repeat belong in one function, in a file of its own that does not end in `.spec.ts`.
- `export` makes a function available to other files, and `import type` brings in a type such as `Page`.
- The helper performs the steps, and every assertion stays in the tests.

## What's next

[Practice](/learn/w2/d1/p4) has you fill the form in the editor, use the helper from a test of your
own, and extend it with a second parameter.

# Week 2 - Day 1 - Practice - Actions on a form

These three problems use the actions from [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2) and the helper function
from [Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3). You write the first one in the editor, and the other two in
your own project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Focus** | Three problems about actions on a form, from Beginner level to Advanced. |
| **Prerequisites** | [Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d1/p2) for the actions, and [Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3) for the helper function. |
| **Environment** | The editor on the right for the first problem, and your own project for the other two. |

## How to answer

Each practice page has three problems, at Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced level. Select
**Start this in the editor** to open a template for a problem, and write your answer on the lines
that start with `//`. Select **Reveal solution** to compare it with a model answer.

## When you are done

You can now fill every kind of control on a form, and find a control that has no label. You can
also keep the steps that fill a form in one function that every test can call.
[Day 2 - Fundamentals](/learn/w2/d2/p2) continues with more ways to find elements and more
assertions to check them.

problems.statement:
**What to build.** Code in the editor that opens the registration form, fills the First Name,
Last Name, and Address fields with values of your own, and shows a screenshot.

**Where.** In the editor, using `launch()` and `show(page)`.

**How you will know it worked.** The screenshot shows your three values in their fields, and the
Console tab shows no error.

**Hint.** The two name fields have placeholder text. The Address field is the only `textarea` on
the page.

**What to build.** A test of your own that uses the helper. In the `tests` folder, create
`practice-register.spec.ts`, with one test that imports `fillRegistrationForm` from
`'./registration-helpers'`, calls it with an email of your own, and checks that the Email field
holds that email.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy your test and the result into the editor,
using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The run reports `1 passed`, and your test contains no `fill()`
line of its own.

**Hint.** Start from the first test in [Implementation](/learn/w2/d1/p3), and change the email in
both places.

**What to build.** A helper that also takes the phone number. In the `tests` folder:

1. In `registration-helpers.ts`, give `fillRegistrationForm` a third parameter, `phone`, and
   fill the Phone field with it. Give the parameter a default value of `'5551234567'`, so that
   `register-helper.spec.ts` still works without a change. A **default value** is written after
   `=` in the parameter list, and it is used when a call leaves that parameter out.
2. Create `practice-phone.spec.ts`, with one test that calls the helper with an email and a phone
   number of your own, and checks that the Phone field holds that number.
3. Run both spec files in one command:
   `npx playwright test tests/register-helper.spec.ts tests/practice-phone.spec.ts --project=chromium`.

**Where.** In VS Code and its integrated terminal. Copy the changed function, your new test, and
the result into the editor, using the template.

**How you will know it worked.** The run reports `3 passed`: the two tests that call the helper
with an email only, and your test that also passes a phone number.

**Hint.** The Phone field is the `<input>` whose `type` attribute is `tel`.
